The greatest common divisor. The greatest common divisor of two integers is the largest positive integer that divides both. Denoted gcd of a and b, it is fundamental to number theory and plays a hidden role in countless algorithms. The Euclidean algorithm efficiently computes it in logarithmic time. It is one of the oldest and most elegant algorithms in mathematics. The greatest common divisor is indispensable for simplifying fractions, solving Diophantine equations, and constructing cryptographic systems.

The greatest common divisor of a and b is the largest positive integer d such that a equals d times m and b equals d times n for some integers m and n. Equivalently, it is the largest divisor common to both a and b. The gcd of a and b divides any linear combination of a and b. This is Bézout's identity: there exist integers x and y, not necessarily unique, with a x plus b y equals gcd of a and b. This is a fundamental result in number theory.

The Euclidean algorithm computes gcd of a and b by repeated division. Gcd of a and b equals gcd of b and a modulo b, repeated until one argument becomes zero. The time complexity is logarithmic in the minimum of a and b, making it extremely efficient. If gcd of a and b equals one, then a and b are coprime or relatively prime. They share no common prime factors and their residues generate the entire multiplicative group modulo their product.

The product gcd of a and b times lcm of a and b equals a times b. This is a beautiful symmetric relationship connecting gcd and lcm. Prime factorization reveals gcd directly. If a and b have prime factorizations, the gcd is found by taking the minimum exponent for each prime factor. The greatest common divisor is essential for cryptography. RSA's security relies on computing phi of p times q when the gcd is tractable for known primes, but factoring remains hard for unknown large primes.

The extended Euclidean algorithm computes not just gcd of a and b but also the Bézout coefficients x and y satisfying a x plus b y equals gcd of a and b. This enables modular inverse computation crucial to cryptography. Applications of gcd permeate mathematics: simplifying fractions, solving linear Diophantine equations, constructing finite fields, and analyzing number-theoretic properties in algebra.
